scope: All 20 source-first findings for chunk 13 individually compared to the actual draft and the lead’s whole-subject/evidence and historical requirement dispositions. Listed parent IDs are semantic destinations, not automatic final-value approvals.

rows.source_first_requirement: Doyle dates counter-revolution proper to the challenge to national sovereignty in June 1789. The Royal Session programme retained orders, privileges and feudal rights while conceding reforms. Later defectors were not welcomed uniformly.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Present with the June sovereignty threshold and programme distinctions. Retain the Royal Session’s substantive concessions as well as preserved orders, and preserve the 303/297/310 source-date discrepancy in auxiliary uncertainty.

rows.source_first_requirement: Artois and courtiers left after July; rural violence, constitutional disappointment, abolition of nobility, army mutiny, suppressed offices and religious reform widened the stream. Turin coordination, Calonne’s wealth and expertise, and weak foreign backing matter separately.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The collective parent and actor records preserve successive waves, organization and foreign limits. Final main content must retain motives beyond mere noble flight and Calonne’s financial/diplomatic contribution; episode-specific evidence must not collapse into a general émigré page union.

rows.source_first_requirement: Favras’s failed rescue conspiracy differs from Mirabeau’s paid advice and plans. Doyle expressly denies that Mirabeau was a counter-revolutionary, although their practical schemes resembled each other. Louis XVI’s refusal to act weakened these projects.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Distinct Favras, Mirabeau and royal-operation routes exist. Preserve Mirabeau’s constitutional purpose, royal inaction and the source’s differing accounts of advice/payment chronology; do not identify all rescue schemes with organized émigré restoration.

rows.source_first_requirement: The Nîmes violence mobilized inherited Catholic-Protestant antagonism sharpened by revolutionary reform. Froment linked it to Artois; Catholic martyrdom deepened royalism. Jalès camps and the premature 1792 rising did not demonstrate a reliable nationwide army.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Nîmes, Jalès and Artois routes preserve regional mobilization and failed capacity. Existing component repairs must keep Froment’s role, the Nîmes-to-Jalès connection and chronology before the national oath schism, rather than representing all southern conflict as its consequence.

rows.source_first_requirement: A proposed Lyon-based royal rescue and southern rising collapsed through non-cooperation and exposure. Cazalès and Maury later cultivated extreme measures in hope of discrediting the new order; this differs from straightforward radical conviction.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Distinct royalist plotting and Assembly obstruction parents retain both arguments. Keep the 1790 plot and later 1795–1796 planning separate from the 1793 federalist revolt, and preserve the tactical purpose of encouraging excess.

rows.source_first_requirement: The failed flight made royal coercion plausible to foreign rulers, increased officer emigration, and accelerated military organization at Koblenz. Pillnitz and subsidies raised hopes, but forces were auxiliaries and ultimately lacked resources and secure bases.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Relevant source arguments and routes exist across parents. Preserve acceleration after Varennes rather than first creation of émigré centres, the failed Black Legion and foreign-subsidy limits, and the conditional character of Pillnitz. The 171/172/173 locator distinctions require exact treatment.

rows.source_first_requirement: The princes’ September 1791 letter denied constitutional legitimacy; the 1793 regency proclamation and Verona in 1795 maintained an intransigent programme. The programme antagonized constitutional royalists and potential allies.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The draft preserves multiple manifesto phases and alienation by Verona. Retain September 1791 rejection, regency and succession separately; the June programme is a later baseline, not an interchangeable date or event.

rows.source_first_requirement: Exile courts reproduced status distinctions and hostility to latecomers, burdening hosts. Doyle also recognizes genuine risk, devotion and willingness of former officers to serve in ranks, exemplified by Chateaubriand.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Hierarchy and factionalism are present, but the final parent stance/content must also preserve genuine devotion, sacrifice and officers’ willingness to serve in ranks. Chateaubriand is an optional illustrative route, not a mandatory separate biography.

rows.source_first_requirement: Disappointment alone did not entail Bourbon restoration. Clerical-oath enforcement, repression and central intrusion helped turn hostility into organized Church-and-king resistance; western conscription was the trigger rather than the complete cause.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The broad and western parents preserve religion, local autonomy and material grievances. Keep the process by which hostility acquired Church-and-king aims and the limited geographic base of mass royalism; conscription is a trigger, not an exhaustive explanation.

rows.source_first_requirement: The Breton association combined provincial attachment, clerical resistance, arms acquisition and links with the princes. Its organizers struggled to keep contacts at home instead of emigrating and lacked a clear operational plan.
rows.independent_reconciliation: A distinct La Rouërie/Breton Association requirement provides the route. Retain provincial attachment, clergy, arms, efforts to keep contacts at home and absent operational plan; do not equate it with Puisaye’s later claimed command.

rows.source_first_requirement: Émigré optimism and Brunswick threats failed to draw popular support. Defeat and retreat broke up most forces, leaving Condé’s units exceptional. War intended to restore royal power instead helped destroy it.
rows.independent_reconciliation: War, manifesto, corps survival and failure parents preserve the causal irony. Retain defeat without implying émigré participation in the Valmy cannonade; distinguish Condé’s exceptional survival and later diaspora from a functioning independent restoration army.

rows.source_first_requirement: British sea power created possibilities for western royalists, but Britain prioritized limiting French power, colonies and strategic footholds. Other powers also resisted permanent commitment to Bourbon objectives. Recognition of Provence was very limited.
rows.independent_reconciliation: British policy, foreign conditionality and dynastic diplomacy provide differentiated access. Preserve actual naval/financial aid alongside strategic priorities, weak recognition and the distinction between émigré complaint and authorial judgment.

rows.source_first_requirement: Light seigneurial burdens, tenancy, rents after tithe abolition, hostility to imposed priests, taxes and intrusive government explain why western peasants saw fewer gains and higher burdens. Vendéans coalesced; Breton chouans remained dispersed.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Main parents preserve multiple grievances and the field-army/guerrilla contrast. Final content must explicitly retain tenancy, rent consequences of tithe abolition and weak gains from seigneurial reform where the source explains western support; general religion/conscription wording alone is insufficient.

rows.source_first_requirement: Opposition to Convention rule did not normally seek old-regime restoration. Royalists exploited Caen and Lyons, while Toulon called the British and declared monarchy chiefly from fear; Hood offered the 1791 constitution, not the princes’ programme.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Federalist and Toulon parents retain republican origins and later conditional royalism. Preserve Hood’s 1791 constitutional offer and fear-driven collaboration; involvement by royalists does not turn all federalism into restorationism.

rows.source_first_requirement: Granville failed to meet Moira’s force; future British help required a port. Puisaye exaggerated both chouan strength and his authority; the guerrillas were disruptive but unable to hold a port. British strategic isolation made his proposal attractive.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The relevant parents retain missed contact, port requirements and inflated claims. Preserve the military distinction between disruptive guerrillas and ability to seize/hold a port; Puisaye’s force totals and authority must remain attributed claims.

rows.source_first_requirement: Mallet du Pan argued revolutionary gains required guarantees and supplied intelligence; d’Antraigues’s rival network altered reports to support uncompromising restoration. Pures and constitutionals also differed internally.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Distinct intelligence and factional parents preserve moderate analysis versus manipulated restorationist reporting. Keep divergent constitutional programmes and customers, not a single reliable royalist intelligence network.

rows.source_first_requirement: Religious toleration, disciplined republican forces, military pressure and supply shortages made 1795 truces possible. Some leaders signed tactically, and not all chouans accepted La Mabilais. Later saturation and executions reduced revolt to precarious peace.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The parents preserve coercion, concessions and tactical agreements. Retain non-universal acceptance of La Mabilais, disciplined suppression of republican abuses, renewed insurgency and precarious peace; toleration alone is not a complete explanation.

rows.source_first_requirement: Poor discipline and unclear command prevented expansion from Quiberon; Hoche’s counterattack captured many and led to executions under émigré laws. Artois arrived too late and the Yeu venture failed to link with Charette. Competing factions blamed Puisaye and Britain.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Separate expedition, follow-up and actor routes exist. Component evidence repairs must keep Quiberon defeat/executions, Yeu failure without battle, Artois’s hesitation and partisan blame distinct; retain the source’s rendered 313 chronology qualification.

rows.source_first_requirement: Rhine schemes envisaged linkage with Lyonnais royalists, but recruitment of Pichegru paralysed action. Bonaparte’s capture of d’Antraigues revealed damaging intelligence in an explicitly murky episode. Louis XVIII was expelled from successive refuges.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The parents preserve planned Rhine/Lyon linkage and Pichegru contacts. Keep the offensive as unrealized, the disclosure episode murky and successive expulsions correctly located; a later implication does not prove successful operational coordination.

rows.source_first_requirement: Factional conflict, incompatible foreign aims, local peasant horizons and republican military power defeated armed restoration by Leoben. Doyle doubts even a royal landing would have induced a western march to Paris. Constitutional monarchy could still gain through elections.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The final failure argument must combine republican force, factionalism, foreign priorities and local horizons while retaining uncertainty about a hypothetical march to Paris. Armed defeat by Leoben is distinct from disappearance of royalism or impossibility of electoral constitutional monarchy.
